# Metric Pitfalls - When Metrics Lie, How to Validate

All numbers in the examples below are hypothetical, for illustration.

## Pitfall 1: Class Imbalance

```
Dataset: 10,000 examples
Frustrated customers: 100 (1%)
Calm customers: 9,900 (99%)

Naive model: "Always predict calm"
Accuracy: 9,900 / 10,000 = 99%

But: Can't detect frustrated at all (recall = 0%)

Why accuracy lied:
Majority class (calm) dominates the metric
Minority class (frustrated) is invisible
```

```
 Always-predict-calm model on that dataset

              Predicted Yes   Predicted No
            ┌──────────────┬───────────────┐
 Actual Yes │   TP = 0     │   FN = 100    │
            ├──────────────┼───────────────┤
 Actual No  │   FP = 0     │   TN = 9,900  │
            └──────────────┴───────────────┘
 Accuracy 99%, recall 0%: the metric hid the failure
```

**Fix: Use precision-recall, not accuracy**

## Pitfall 2: Metric Gaming

```
Researcher tweaks the threshold to maximize F1 on
the test set
F1 = 0.95 (amazing!)

Deploy to production:
F1 = 0.72 (horrible, what happened?)

Why metric gamed:
- Threshold tuned to the test set (overfit to those
  specific examples)
- Production may have a different distribution,
  class ratio, and data quality
```

**Fix: Hold-out test set (don't tune on it)**

## Pitfall 3: Distribution Shift

```
Model trained on data that was 60% female, 40% male
Deployed later to traffic that is 50% / 50%

Frustration detection accuracy on women: 92%
Frustration detection accuracy on men: 78%

Model performs worse on men (possibly not enough
training data for that group)

Why metric lied:
- Metric averages across groups
- Hidden performance degradation on one group
- Only noticed when disaggregating
```

**Fix: Stratified evaluation (per subgroup)**

## Pitfall 4: Calibration (Confidence ≠ Correctness)

```
Toy example, three predictions:
  Example 1: 95% confidence "frustrated" → actually calm
  Example 2: 95% confidence "calm" → actually frustrated
  Example 3: 95% confidence "frustrated" → frustrated

Accuracy: 1 of 3 correct = 33%
Stated confidence: 95% on average

Problem:
Model says "I'm 95% sure" but is right far less often
Confidence is not calibrated to accuracy
```

**Fix: Calibration curve (is model's confidence honest?)**

```
Binned by stated confidence (hypothetical):
Bar = actual accuracy of the model in that bin

 90-100% │███████████████████████████████████░░░░░ 85%
 80-90%  │███████████████████████████████░░░░░░░░░ 78%
 70-80%  │█████████████████████████████░░░░░░░░░░░ 71%
         └─────────────────────────────────────────
          0%        25%        50%        75%  100%

Well calibrated: bar lands inside the stated range.
Top two bins fall below their range: overconfident.
The 70-80% bin is fine.
```

Calibration can be measured (expected calibration error) and repaired after training, for example with temperature scaling or isotonic regression fitted on a validation set. A calibration curve says how far to trust the confidence; it does not make the model more accurate.

## Pitfall 5: Wrong Metric for the Task

```
Ranking task: "Which customer is most frustrated?"

Model A: AUC=0.95 (a random frustrated call is
         scored above a random calm call 95% of the time)
Model B: AUC=0.92

Choose Model A? Maybe not.

If only the top 10 customers matter:
  Model A: Gets 8 of top 10 frustrated
  Model B: Gets 9 of top 10 frustrated
  
  Model B is better for this use case
  AUC didn't capture it (AUC looks at full ranking)
```

**Fix: Use a top-k metric: precision@10, or NDCG@10 (normalized DCG at top 10) when relevance has grades**

## Validation: The Real Test

```
 all labeled data (e.g. 1000 recordings)
 ┌───────────────────────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
 │ train 60%                 │ val 20%  │ test 20% │
 │ fit the model             │ tune     │ report   │
 └───────────────────────────┴──────────┴──────────┘
  Split by customer or call so the same speaker never
  lands on both sides (that leaks).
```

```
Development cycle:
  1. Train on training set (60%)
  2. Tune hyperparameters on validation set (20%)
  3. Report final metrics on test set (20%)

Never tune on test set!

For a speech-emotion model (evaluation):
  1. Collect 1000 call recordings
  2. Split: 600 train, 200 val, 200 test
  3. Train tone_v2.3 on 600
  4. Tune on 200 val (if needed)
  5. Report F1 on 200 test (hold this sacred)
  6. Compare tone_v2.2 vs tone_v2.3 on same 200 test
  
  Result: Fair comparison, no gaming
```

Watch the test set size against class balance: with 1% positives, 200 test examples contain about 2 frustrated calls, so F1 on them is nearly meaningless. Stratify the split and size the test set by number of positives, and report confidence intervals. Comparing many model versions on one test set also slowly overfits to it.

## Interview Pattern: Metric Pitfalls

```
Q: "Your ML model has 98% accuracy on test set.
   But in production, it underperforms. Why?"

Weak answer:
  "Data drift, need to retrain"
  (❌ Maybe, but not diagnosing the root cause)

Strong answer:
  "Multiple possibilities:
  
  1. Check if accuracy was meaningful:
     - What's the baseline (always predict majority)?
     - Frustration label: 1% frustrated, 99% calm
     - Baseline accuracy: 99%
     - Model accuracy: 98% (worse than baseline!)
  
  2. Check for overfitting on test set:
     - Was the test set metric tuned?
     - If yes: need a separate hold-out test set
  
  3. Check for distribution shift:
     - Training data: one call center (specific
       accents, language)
     - Production: a different customer base
     - Disaggregate by region, age, language
     - e.g. 98% overall but far lower on a new region
  
  4. Check for calibration:
     - Model says 98% confident
     - But is right much less often than that
     - Overconfident: scores can't be trusted
  
  5. Check for metric mismatch:
     - Optimized accuracy (average case)
     - But production cares about recall (catch all
       frustrated customers)
     - Need precision-recall or F1
  
  6. Diagnosis approach:
     a) Collect a new hold-out set (never seen)
     b) Disaggregate (by region, demographics, etc.)
     c) Confusion matrix (precision, recall, F1)
     d) Check calibration (is confidence honest?)
     e) Compare to baseline (better than naive?)
  
  My guess: distribution shift + metric mismatch
  - 98% accuracy is misleading
  - Real metric = precision-recall or F1 (lower)
  - Measure on fresh production-like data before
    claiming any number"

Why this signals good judgment:
  - You didn't just blame data drift
  - You understood metric can be misleading
  - You had a diagnostic approach (disaggregate,
    check calibration)
  - You'd set up proper evaluation (hold-out, no tuning)
```

## Checklist: ML Evaluation in Production

- [ ] Choose metric by business goal (not just accuracy)
- [ ] Hold-out test set (never tune on it)
- [ ] Stratified evaluation (check per-subgroup performance)
- [ ] Calibration curve (is confidence honest?)
- [ ] Disaggregate metrics (find hidden problems)
- [ ] Baseline (is model better than naive?)
- [ ] Monitor for drift (does metric change in production?)

## What This Signals

- You've debugged model underperformance (know the pitfalls)
- You understand metrics can mislead (accuracy alone is dangerous)
- You have a robust evaluation process (hold-out test, disaggregation)
- You think about real-world impact (not just test-set numbers)
